title: Justice (ST II-II.58)

segments.voice: Yesterday, prudence: right reason applied to action, ending not in thinking but in doing. Your line was think, then act.

The neighbor's ladder has been leaning in the garage since spring. It was borrowed for one afternoon. Nobody's angry. Nobody's even asked for it back. But every time the garage door goes up, there it is, quietly saying something. Or a coworker's idea saved the project, and in the big meeting it somehow came out sounding like yours. Nobody lied, exactly. But something is owed and hasn't been paid. Today Thomas names the virtue that faces outward, toward everyone else. Justice.
screen: `A BORROWED LADDER, STILL HERE.` → `AN IDEA THAT WASN'T YOURS.` → `SOMETHING IS OWED.`

segments.voice: Thomas takes his definition from the old Roman lawyers and makes it his own. Justice is a habit by which a person, with a constant and lasting will, gives to each one their due. Look at the pieces. To each one: not just the people you like, or the ones who can pay you back. Their due: what belongs to them. Credit for their work. The truth. Wages on time. A fair hearing. Their ladder. Then the word that's easiest to skip: constant. One fair act on a good day isn't yet the virtue. Justice is being the kind of person who returns what's owed as a matter of course, the habit from two days ago, aimed outward. Here's what sets it apart. The other moral virtues, Thomas says, set a person right inside: calm when angry, brave when afraid. Justice is always about someone else. It's the virtue of the relationship; you can't do it alone in a room. And Thomas widens the circle as far as it goes. Even God is owed something: honor, worship, thanks. Jesus says it in one breath, in the Douay-Rheims: "Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar's; and to God, the things that are God's." Justice, for Thomas, isn't first a courtroom or a protest sign, though it reaches both. It starts with the ladder in the garage.
screen: `TO EACH ONE, THEIR DUE.` · `A CONSTANT AND LASTING WILL.` · `ALWAYS ABOUT SOMEONE ELSE.` · `EVEN GOD IS OWED SOMETHING.` · then, large: `RENDER TO GOD THE THINGS THAT ARE GOD'S.`

segments.voice: Let the people around you come to mind one at a time: family, coworkers, a neighbor, the person who serves you coffee. For each, ask quietly whether there's something you owe and haven't given: thanks, credit, a returned call, money, an apology, a fair hearing for someone you've written off. Let the clearest one rise to the top, and if you pray, name that person before God.
Justice. For Thomas, a steady will to give each person what is their due, a virtue that always faces someone else. Today's word.
Your line: each their due. The thanks and the credit count as much as the ladder. Day one thousand one hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching counts justice among the four cardinal virtues, describing it as the constant will to give God and neighbor their due, and Catholic social teaching applies it to wages, work and the common good.

chat.meaning: For Thomas, justice is a constant will to give each one their due: credit, truth, wages, even worship to God. It reaches courtrooms, but starts at home.

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased.
